covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832.

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000a.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('5.85×10² milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('1.3 milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: meteoritic (CI-chondrite) value; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

crystal.reference: Pauling, L.; Keaveny, I.; Robinson, A. B. (1970). Journal of Solid State Chemistry 2, 225.
crystal.note: Low-temperature solid only, at 23 K. CIF note: the α phase is stable below 45.6 K.

production.basis: mine production, fluorspar (gross weight, all grades)

tonnesPerYear.note: World mine production, fluorspar (gross weight, all grades), 2025 (USGS: 10,000 thousand metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, average unit value of imports, cost, insurance, and freight, dollars per metric ton: Acid grade [Fluorspar], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

critical.note: Fluorspar (fluorite, CaF2) is a mineral and the main industrial source of fluorine (via hydrofluoric acid); listed as the mineral.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.501, massive_stars 0.499); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 48 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: '51% of F ... produced by AGB stars' (figure reading 0.501).

humanRole.text: Strengthens tooth enamel against decay; EFSA sets an adequate intake for this reason but does not consider it essential.

isotopeUses.text: Fluorine-18 in a glucose analogue (FDG), first made in 1978 to measure how much sugar the brain uses: cells take it up like glucose but cannot use it further, so it collects where they are most active, which a PET scanner then sees.

history.discoveredText: 1771 (in hydrofluoric acid; the element was isolated in 1886)
history.nameOrigin: From fluorspar (fluorite), whose name comes from the Latin fluere, 'to flow', because miners added the mineral to ores to help them melt.
history.note: PubChem's YearDiscovered (1670) is the date of the earliest known use of a fluorine compound to etch glass, not of the element. Los Alamos prints the isolation year as 1866, a slip for 1886. Moissan isolated the gas by electrolysis in a platinum apparatus.

prose.text: Fluorine is a pale-yellow, poisonous gas and the most reactive of all elements; we meet it tamed, as fluoride in toothpaste, in non-stick pan coatings and in the mineral fluorite. Fluorite often glows under ultraviolet light, and it lent its name both to the element and to the word 'fluorescence'. A fluorine atom, [He] 2s² 2p⁵, is one electron short of a closed shell (ground term ²P°₃/₂), and it pulls on shared electrons harder than any other atom, with the highest Pauling electronegativity, 3.98. Its only stable isotope, fluorine-19, has nuclear spin 1/2, which makes fluorine-containing drugs easy to follow by NMR.
